question: Can a gift deed executed by a very old man in favour of his grandson be set aside for undue influence merely because of their close relationship and the donor's age?
facts: A man in his late eighties executed a registered gift deed transferring part of his land to his only grandson, who lived with him. After his death, his sons sued to cancel the deed, pleading that given the relationship and the donor's great age the court should presume undue influence and put the grandson to proof that the gift was the donor's free act. There was no evidence that the donor was of unsound mind or that the grandson controlled his affairs.
gold_issues: Does a close family relationship between donor and donee, or the donor's old age, by itself raise a presumption of undue influence under s. 16 of the Contract Act?
On whom does the burden of proof lie, and when does it shift to the donee?

gold_supporting_authorities.title: Subhas Chandra Das Mushib v. Ganga Prosad Das Mushib
gold_supporting_authorities.proposition: There is no presumption of undue influence merely because donor and donee are near relations; the court must first find that the donee was in a position to dominate the donor's will and used it to obtain an unfair advantage.

gold_supporting_authorities.title: Ladli Prasad Jaiswal v. Karnal Distillery Co. Ltd.
gold_supporting_authorities.proposition: Section 16(3) raises a rebuttable presumption, shifting the burden to the party benefiting, only when he is proved to be in a position to dominate the will of the other and the transaction appears unconscionable; undue influence must be pleaded with particulars and cannot be inferred from facts never pleaded and proved.

gold_contrary_authorities.title: Krishna Mohan Kul v. Pratima Maity
gold_contrary_authorities.proposition: Where the beneficiary stood in a fiduciary relationship with a very aged executant, the onus to prove the validity of the deed was on the beneficiary.

key_points: Section 16(1) requires both a position to dominate the will and use of that position to obtain an unfair advantage.
Relationship or age alone does not raise a presumption; s. 16(2) lists situations where domination may be found.
The burden shifts under s. 16(3) only once domination is shown and the transaction appears unconscionable.
Fiduciary relationships and extreme age or infirmity can shift the onus (the contrary line of cases).
notes: A gift is not a contract, but the Court applies s. 16 principles to gifts inter vivos (Subhas Chandra, h-2).

question: Can sisters set aside a family partition and consent decree on a general allegation that their signatures were obtained by fraud?
facts: Years after a partition of family property was recorded in a consent decree and acted upon, two sisters sued their brothers to set aside the partition and a release deed, alleging in general terms that their signatures were obtained by fraud and misrepresentation. The plaint gave no particulars of what was misrepresented, by whom or when. The documents had been signed with their knowledge.
gold_issues: What must a party plead and prove to avoid a transaction for fraud or misrepresentation?
Can a consent decree acted upon be reopened on vague allegations of fraud?

gold_supporting_authorities.title: Ranganayakamma v. K.S. Prakash
gold_supporting_authorities.proposition: When fraud is alleged its particulars must be pleaded (Order 6 Rule 4 CPC); general and vague allegations of fraud or misrepresentation cannot found relief against a consent decree that was acted upon.

key_points: Fraud (s. 17) and misrepresentation (s. 18) make a contract voidable (s. 19).
Particulars of fraud must be pleaded; without them evidence cannot be led.
A decree or partition acted upon for years binds the parties unless fraud is proved.

question: Can an employer enforce a clause stopping a former employee from working for a competitor in the same city for two years after leaving?
facts: A valuation firm's service agreement barred its branch manager, for two years after leaving the firm's service, from serving any competitor or starting a similar business within the city where he last worked. He resigned and joined a competing firm in that city. The firm sued for an injunction.
gold_issues: Is a post-employment covenant not to compete void under s. 27 of the Contract Act?
Does reasonableness of the restraint (time, place) save it, as it might in English law?

gold_supporting_authorities.title: Superintendence Company of India (P) Ltd. v. Krishan Murgai
gold_supporting_authorities.proposition: The majority held that a post-service covenant worded for an employee who leaves could not be enforced where his service was terminated; A.P. Sen J. held that such covenants fall within s. 27, since the doctrine of restraint of trade applies only once the contract of employment ends.

gold_supporting_authorities.title: Percept D'Mark (India) Pvt. Ltd. v. Zaheer Khan
gold_supporting_authorities.proposition: The reading of s. 27 under which post-contractual restraints are void has been uniform since 1874, and the Court declined to reopen it (at the interlocutory stage, without a final view on the merits).

gold_contrary_authorities.title: Niranjan Shankar Golikari v. Century Spinning and Mfg. Co. Ltd.
gold_contrary_authorities.proposition: Negative covenants operating during the term of employment are not restraints of trade under s. 27 and can be enforced.

key_points: Section 27 voids every agreement restraining a lawful profession, trade or business, except the sale-of-goodwill exception.
Indian law does not save a post-employment restraint because it is reasonable.
Restraints during the term of employment are treated differently (Golikari).
An injunction should be refused.
notes: Percept D'Mark was an interlocutory appeal (the Court kept all contentions open, p-78); it is cited for the settled reading of s. 27, not as a final ruling on its clause.

question: Is a long-term power supply contract frustrated, or excused by force majeure, because a foreign law change made the contracted fuel much more expensive?
facts: A generator agreed to supply electricity to a State utility for 25 years at a fixed tariff, planning to burn coal imported from Indonesia. Indonesia later changed its law so that coal could not be exported below international market prices, sharply raising the generator's costs. The contract's force majeure clause covered events that prevent performance. The generator sought release from the tariff.
gold_issues: Does a steep rise in the cost of performance make a contract impossible under s. 56?
Can a force majeure clause covering events that "prevent" performance be invoked for higher costs?

gold_supporting_authorities.title: Energy Watchdog v. Central Electricity Regulatory Commission
gold_supporting_authorities.proposition: A rise in the price of fuel does not frustrate a contract whose fundamental basis is unaltered, and force majeure clauses are narrowly construed.

gold_supporting_authorities.title: Satyabrata Ghose v. Mugneeram Bangur & Co.
gold_supporting_authorities.proposition: "Impossible" in s. 56 means impracticable from the point of view of the object the parties had in view, not merely more onerous.

gold_supporting_authorities.title: Alopi Parshad & Sons Ltd. v. Union of India
gold_supporting_authorities.proposition: Courts cannot absolve a party from performance because it has become onerous through an unforeseen turn of events.

key_points: Section 56 covers supervening impossibility in a practical sense, as a rule of positive law.
Increased cost or commercial hardship does not frustrate a contract.
Force majeure clauses are construed narrowly; a clause triggered by prevention is not triggered by higher costs.
The generator remains bound by the tariff (subject to any change-in-law clause).

question: Must an employer prove actual loss before deducting agreed liquidated damages for late delivery under a supply contract?
facts: A public sector oil company bought pipes for an offshore project. The contract said that for delay the buyer would recover, as agreed liquidated damages and not as a penalty, 1% of the contract price per week, being a genuine pre-estimate of damages. Delivery was late and the buyer deducted the amount. The supplier argued that the buyer had to prove the loss it actually suffered.
gold_issues: Is proof of actual loss necessary to recover a sum stipulated as liquidated damages under s. 74?
When is a stipulated sum a penalty rather than a genuine pre-estimate?

gold_supporting_authorities.title: Oil & Natural Gas Corporation Ltd. v. Saw Pipes Ltd.
gold_supporting_authorities.proposition: If the sum named is a genuine pre-estimate of loss, the party need not prove actual loss, particularly where loss is difficult to prove; if it is a penalty, only reasonable compensation is recoverable.

gold_supporting_authorities.title: Fateh Chand v. Balkishan Das
gold_supporting_authorities.proposition: Section 74 caps recovery at reasonable compensation not exceeding the sum named, whether the stipulation is a penalty or liquidated damages.

gold_contrary_authorities.title: Kailash Nath Associates v. Delhi Development Authority
gold_contrary_authorities.proposition: Damage or loss caused by the breach is a sine qua non for applying s. 74; where loss can be proved it must be.

key_points: Section 74 does away with the English penalty/liquidated damages distinction for recovery; only reasonable compensation up to the sum named is recoverable.
A genuine pre-estimate can be taken as the measure without proof of actual loss where loss is hard to prove.
Where loss can be proved, it must be proved (Kailash Nath).
Delay in a public project is a case where loss is hard to quantify.
notes: Saw Pipes arose from an arbitral award; Kailash Nath later restated the s. 74 principles and should be reconciled with it.

question: Can the Government forfeit a large security deposit on a supply contract after the supplier defaults, without showing any loss?
facts: A contractor agreed to supply goods to the Government and deposited security for due performance; the contract said the deposit would be forfeited if he neglected to perform. He defaulted on some deliveries, the Government rescinded the contract and forfeited the whole deposit, and led no evidence of loss even though it could have bought replacement goods in the market.
gold_issues: Is forfeiture of a security deposit a stipulation by way of penalty under s. 74?
Must the party forfeiting prove loss where loss is capable of proof?

gold_supporting_authorities.title: Fateh Chand v. Balkishan Das
gold_supporting_authorities.proposition: "Any other stipulation by way of penalty" in s. 74 covers forfeiture of money already paid; the court awards only reasonable compensation.

gold_supporting_authorities.title: Maula Bux v. Union of India
gold_supporting_authorities.proposition: A deposit for due performance is not earnest money; its forfeiture is subject to s. 74, and where loss can be proved the party must prove it.

gold_supporting_authorities.title: Kailash Nath Associates v. Delhi Development Authority
gold_supporting_authorities.proposition: Loss caused by the breach is a sine qua non for compensation under s. 74.

gold_contrary_authorities.title: Satish Batra v. Sudhir Rawal
gold_contrary_authorities.proposition: Money that is truly earnest money under clear terms can be forfeited on default.

key_points: Forfeiture of a deposit is a stipulation by way of penalty covered by s. 74.
Only reasonable compensation, up to the amount forfeited, is recoverable.
Loss that can be proved (market purchase) must be proved.
Distinguish earnest money (a reasonable pledge) from a security deposit.

topic: time as the essence (sale of land)
question: Is time of the essence of an agreement to sell a house because it fixes ten days for paying the second instalment, so that the seller may cancel if it is not paid?
facts: An agreement to sell a house required the buyer to pay a large second instalment within ten days, the balance at registration. The seller was to redeem a mortgage and obtain an income-tax clearance. The buyer did not pay within ten days, insisting that the seller first redeem the mortgage. The seller treated the contract as ended; the buyer sued for specific performance.
gold_issues: Is time of the essence in a contract for the sale of immovable property?
Can a stipulated time for a payment make time essential for that payment?

gold_supporting_authorities.title: Chand Rani v. Kamal Rani
gold_supporting_authorities.proposition: In sales of immovable property time is presumed not to be of the essence; the presumption is displaced by unmistakable language or by the nature of the property, the parties' conduct and the surrounding circumstances, and time can be essential for a particular payment.

gold_supporting_authorities.title: Saradamani Kandappan v. S. Rajalakshmi
gold_supporting_authorities.proposition: Where time is specified for payment of the consideration, time can be of the essence for payment even though not for execution of the sale deed; the old presumption should be applied with regard to rising prices.

key_points: The presumption against time being essential in land sales, and how it is displaced.
Time can be essential for one obligation (a payment) and not others.
A party who insists on the other's performance first, contrary to the agreed order, is not ready and willing.
Under s. 55, failure to perform at a time that is essential makes the contract voidable by the other party.

question: Must a State Government pay for construction work it accepted and used, although the contract was not executed in the form required by Article 299 of the Constitution?
facts: A contractor built structures for the State on the oral or informal instructions of an officer. No contract in the form required by Article 299 was executed. The State used the buildings but refused to pay, arguing that there was no valid contract.
gold_issues: Is a contract with the Government that does not comply with Article 299 enforceable?
Can the contractor claim compensation under s. 70 of the Contract Act?

gold_supporting_authorities.title: State of West Bengal v. B.K. Mondal & Sons
gold_supporting_authorities.proposition: Where a person lawfully does work for the Government not intending to do so gratuitously and the Government enjoys the benefit, s. 70 obliges it to compensate, and the constitutional formality does not bar that claim.

gold_supporting_authorities.title: Mulamchand v. State of Madhya Pradesh
gold_supporting_authorities.proposition: A contract not complying with Article 299 is void, but s. 70 can found a claim for restitution, provided the claimant accounts for what he himself received under the transaction.

key_points: Contracts not in Article 299 form are void and cannot be enforced by either side.
Section 70 requires lawful doing, no intention to act gratuitously, and enjoyment of the benefit.
Liability under s. 70 is quasi-contractual, not based on the void contract.
The claimant must account for benefits he received (Mulamchand).

question: Can a bank recover the guaranteed debt from the guarantor without first proceeding against the principal debtor or the mortgaged property?
facts: A bank lent to a firm against a mortgage of a shop and a personal guarantee. The firm defaulted and the bank obtained a decree against the firm, the guarantor, and the mortgaged shop. In execution it proceeded first against the guarantor, who objected that the bank must first sell the mortgaged shop and exhaust its remedies against the principal debtor.
gold_issues: Is the surety's liability co-extensive with the principal debtor's under s. 128?
Must the creditor exhaust remedies against the principal debtor or security first?

gold_supporting_authorities.title: Bank of Bihar Ltd. v. Damodar Prasad
gold_supporting_authorities.proposition: The surety's liability is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor and immediate; absent a special equity the creditor need not first exhaust remedies against the principal.

gold_supporting_authorities.title: State Bank of India v. Indexport Registered
gold_supporting_authorities.proposition: A decree against the principal debtor and guarantor jointly and severally may be executed against the guarantor first; nothing requires the mortgaged property to be proceeded against first.

key_points: Under s. 128 the surety's liability is co-extensive with the principal debtor's, unless the contract provides otherwise.
The creditor may choose whom to proceed against.
The surety's rights of subrogation and indemnity (ss. 140, 145) protect him after payment.

question: Is a clause in a Government company's service rules allowing it to terminate a permanent employee on three months' notice without reason enforceable?
facts: Rules of a Government-owned corporation, incorporated into every employee's contract, allowed the corporation to end a permanent employee's service at any time on three months' notice or pay, without stating any reason. Employees had no real choice but to accept the rules. Two employees were terminated under the clause and challenged it.
gold_issues: Is an unconscionable term in a standard-form contract between parties of unequal bargaining power void under s. 23?
Does it matter that the employer is a Government company (Article 14)?

gold_supporting_authorities.title: Central Inland Water Transport Corporation Ltd. v. Brojo Nath Ganguly
gold_supporting_authorities.proposition: Courts will not enforce, and will strike down, an unfair and unreasonable clause in a contract between parties of unequal bargaining power; a clause giving absolute and arbitrary power to terminate is opposed to public policy and void under s. 23.

key_points: Section 23 voids agreements whose object or consideration is opposed to public policy.
Public policy includes protection against unconscionable terms imposed through unequal bargaining power (standard-form contracts).
The clause conferred arbitrary power without guidelines.
As a Government company is "the State", Article 14 also applies.
notes: The Court limited the principle to cases of real inequality of bargaining power and did not extend it to commercial transactions between equals.
